# Draft:Traditional wet shaving terminology

----
Traditional wet shaving terminology describes abbreviations, jargon, and equipment terms commonly used by enthusiasts of wet shaving—especially in online communities discussing safety razor shaving, straight razor shaving, and lather-building with brush and soap/cream. Terms often describe shaving direction (relative to hair growth), closeness of results, razor head designs, and community practices such as sharing or trading equipment.
Overview
Traditional wet shaving typically refers to shaving with water-based lather (often built with a brush) and a razor such as a safety razor, straight razor, or shavette. As with many hobbyist communities, wet shavers use shorthand to describe routines, results, and gear, including standardized abbreviations for pass direction and informal slang for collecting habits.
Common abbreviations
The following abbreviations are widely used in wet shaving discussions and guides. Terminology and nuance can vary between communities.
{| class="wikitable"
! Abbreviation !! Meaning !! Notes
|-
| WTG || With the grain || Shaving in the same direction as hair growth.
|-
| XTG || Across the grain || Shaving roughly perpendicular to hair growth.
|-
| ATG || Against the grain || Shaving opposite hair growth; often closest, sometimes most irritating.
|-
| Pass || A complete shave pass in one direction || Multiple passes (e.g., WTG then XTG) are commonly used to reduce stubble gradually.
|-
| BBS || Baby butt smooth || Very close shave with little or no detectable stubble.
|-
| DFS || Damn/Darn fine shave || Close shave that may fall short of BBS.
|-
| CCS || Close comfortable shave || Comfortable, close shave; typically less close than DFS.
|-
| SAS || Socially acceptable shave || Presentable result with some detectable stubble.
|-
| DE || Double-edge (safety razor) || Uses a thin blade sharpened on two edges.
|-
| SE || Single-edge (razor) || Uses a blade with one cutting edge; formats vary by system and model.
|-
| OC / CC || Open comb / closed comb || Refers to safety razor guard style (teeth vs safety bar).
|-
| TTO || Twist-to-open || Safety razor mechanism that opens doors/top-cap by twisting the handle (common in some vintage designs).
|-
| HTT || Hot towel treatment || Pre-shave preparation using a hot towel to soften beard hair.
|-
| YMMV || Your mileage may vary || Indicates results differ by person/skin/technique.
|-
| SOTD || Shave of the day || Posts sharing the day’s shave setup and products.
|-
| PIF || Pay it forward || Gifting gear or samples to others in the community rather than selling.
|-
| NOS || New old stock || Unused vintage item, often collected for rarity or performance claims.
|-
| WTB / WTT / FS / FT || Want to buy / want to trade / for sale / for trade || Marketplace shorthand used on forums and hobbyist exchanges.
|}
Technique and hair-growth terms
Grain mapping
Grain refers to the direction that hair grows on different parts of the face and neck. Many shavers “map” their grain to plan WTG/XTG/ATG passes and reduce irritation.
Advanced finishing techniques
Some wet shavers use specialized strokes to remove stubborn stubble, such as short buffing strokes or diagonal “sliding” movements. These approaches are typically considered advanced and may increase irritation if used with poor technique.
Razor and razor-design terms
Open comb vs closed comb
In safety razors, an open-comb design uses teeth or gaps along the guard, while a closed-comb (often called a safety bar) uses a continuous bar. Open comb designs are commonly described as more efficient on longer growth due to improved lather/hair channeling, though perceived aggressiveness depends on multiple factors.
Blade gap and aggressiveness
Blade gap generally refers to the distance between the blade edge and the safety bar/guard area; larger gaps are often associated with a more aggressive feel, though shaving comfort depends on geometry, exposure, and technique.
Brush and lather terms
Blooming (soap)
Blooming commonly refers to soaking a hard shaving soap with water before loading the brush, intended to soften the surface and sometimes intensify fragrance. Some shavers consider it helpful while others consider it unnecessary, depending on water hardness and soap formulation.
Soap, cream, and croap
Shaving products are often described as:
* Soap – a more solid product loaded onto a wet brush
* Cream – a softer product that typically lathers quickly
* Croap – an informal blend term meaning a soft soap / firm cream consistency (community usage varies).
Post-shave and minor-cut treatment
Aftershave
Aftershave products (splashes, balms, or lotions) are used after shaving to soothe skin, reduce discomfort, and support healing of minor irritation. Alcohol-based products may disinfect but can be drying; many modern formulas emphasize soothing ingredients.
Alum block
An alum block (commonly potassium alum) is used by some shavers as an astringent/antiseptic step after shaving to reduce irritation and help with minor nicks.
Styptic pencil
A styptic pencil is a targeted product applied to small cuts to help stop bleeding by constricting tissue and supporting clotting; it is typically used only on individual nicks rather than over the whole face.
Straight-razor maintenance
Strop
A razor strop (often leather) is used to align and polish a straight razor’s edge between honings; stropping is generally described as maintenance rather than sharpening.
Lathering vessels
Scuttle
A shaving scuttle is a two-piece or double-walled vessel intended to keep lather warm during shaving (often by surrounding the lather bowl with hot water).
Community culture
Wet shaving communities often include recurring post formats (e.g., SOTD posts), hobbyist trading/gifting (PIF), and humorous shorthand for collecting behavior (e.g., “acquisition disorders”), reflecting the hobby’s blend of grooming practice and collecting culture.
